title: Wider Than the Arithmetic
passage:
The hall is cold, and the upright against the end wall has not been opened since the spring. Pauline Jerrowsett has the top off it and a wedge of felt in against two of its three strings; she strikes the note, moves the lever by less than a degree, and strikes it again.

Before starting she played a dozen notes into her meter, the last of them from the top octave, and it drew her a curve for all eighty-eight notes from this piano’s own figure.

A piano string is stiff, and a stiff wire’s partials – the quieter tones above the note you hear – run sharp of the whole-number multiples the sums expect. The shorter and thicker the wire, the further out they go, so this upright’s figure is larger than a grand’s, its short thick strings already counted in it. A note down in the tenor has its fourth partial about nine cents sharp, and that is where the treble note two octaves above it goes, nine cents wide of the arithmetic.

She follows the curve through the middle of the keyboard. In the top octave and a half she goes past it, by two or three cents. “The curve’s right about the wire,” she says. “What it can’t know is that nobody plays up there on its own. The last octave comes in over somebody’s left hand, two octaves down, and that’s what it has to agree with.”

Further than that she will not go. “Stretch the middle to match,” she says, “and the thirds inside a chord start to grind. That’s most of what anybody hears all evening.” The extra cents are not an allowance for the cold: a winter takes the whole instrument down together, and that is another visit.

She screws the top back on. Inside the lid, under four other dates in four other hands, she pencils today’s.

– Zena Medhurst

questions.prompt: What, according to the text, is Jerrowsett’s reason for going past her meter’s curve in the top octave?

options.text: Her meter took its dozen notes from the middle of the keyboard, and its curve stops where they stop.
A small instrument loses more to the stiffness of its wire than the figure allows for.

questions.rationale:
Option D is the key, and Jerrowsett gives the reason herself. She is not correcting the meter: “The curve’s right about the wire,” she says, so what she adds at the top is not a repair to a figure she thinks wrong. Her reason is about how those notes are listened to rather than about how they vibrate. “What it can’t know is that nobody plays up there on its own. The last octave comes in over somebody’s left hand, two octaves down, and that’s what it has to agree with.” D puts that in other words: the last notes arrive over a hand playing two octaves lower and have to be in tune with it, which is why they end up above the figure her meter supplies.

Option A is the picture a reader builds of a machine fed a handful of notes – that it speaks for the stretch of keyboard it was fed from, and that the top is therefore the tuner’s own business. Two spans rule it out. The notes she played in were not confined to the middle: “Before starting she played a dozen notes into her meter, the last of them from the top octave”. And what came out of them covers the instrument: “it drew her a curve for all eighty-eight notes from this piano’s own figure”. The curve reaches the last octave. She goes past it there, which is a different act from filling a gap.

Option B borrows a true sentence from the passage and asks it to explain the wrong thing. Short thick wire does lose more to stiffness – “The shorter and thicker the wire, the further out they go” – and this upright’s figure is the larger one for that reason. But the figure is not blind to it: “so this upright’s figure is larger than a grand’s, its short thick strings already counted in it.” The small instrument’s share of stiffness is inside the number she has been given, not left outside it for her to supply.

Option C is where a reader lands who recognises that pianos drift with the season; the passage grants the drift itself. What it refuses is the link to the top octave: “The extra cents are not an allowance for the cold: a winter takes the whole instrument down together, and that is another visit.” A cold hall moves the whole instrument at once; the two or three cents she adds are at one end of it, and she says what they are for.

The mechanism runs one way, and the way it runs is easy to lose. A stiff string’s partials sit above the whole-number multiples rather than below them, so a treble note matched to the fourth partial of a note two octaves down finishes above the sums and not under them. The octave is left wide on purpose, and that is how an instrument tuned as it should be measures as one tuned wrong.

hazard_probe.factual_check_of_the_written_mechanism: Each claim in the passage was checked against the sources above before it was written down. Stiffness raises the partials above whole-number multiples (encyclopaedia, verbatim: harmonic frequencies are ‘slightly higher, and proportionately more so in the higher than in the lower harmonics’). Shorter and thicker wire gives more of it, so a small upright's figure exceeds a grand's (encyclopaedia, on spinets against concert grands). Matching a treble note to the fourth partial of a note two octaves below is the double-octave check a tuner uses, and about nine cents on that partial is the right order for a short-scale upright. An electronic device measuring inharmonicity from sampled notes and computing a whole-keyboard curve is what the TuneLab and patent material describes. The trade-off stated in her second quotation – widen the middle to match and the thirds inside a chord beat faster – follows from widening the temperament octave and is the standard reason a tuner stops.
